newsitem.title: GERMANY: Adams says Irish peace talks confidence collapsed.
newsitem.headline: Adams says Irish peace talks confidence collapsed.

text.p: Irish Republican leader Gerry Adams said on Thursday that confidence in the faltering Northern Ireland peace talks had collapsed.
With Protestant guerrillas threatening to end their ceasefire in the British province, he added: "When you have a vacuum, I do think it will be filled by these type of developments."

The president of Sinn Fein, political wing of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), said the push for peace should not be allowed to slacken off in the lead-up to the next British general election due by next May.
"We cannot take a sabbatical, we cannot take time off," he told Reuters in an interview at the Frankfurt Book Fair, where he was publicising his autobiography "Before The Dawn".

The IRA unilaterally ended its 17-month truce in February this year, shattering the calm with a bomb attack in London. Adams refused to speculate on the possibility of the republican guerrillas calling a new ceasefire.

Protestant guerrillas, who want to maintain Northern Ireland's links with Britain, have grown dissatisfied with the lack of progress in the peace process, raising fears that they too might end their truce.
Protestant politicians demanding that the IRA scrap its arms before Sinn Fein is given a seat at the talks have also accused the London and Dublin governments of caving in to the guerrilla group.
Adams said of the talks: "There isn't any confidence in them even by the two governments if they would admit it."

"We warned about the vacuum that had been created and I think that all we have seen in the last number of days has vindicated that. I say that rather sadly as there is no one I know who is triumphalistic or pleased."
"People on the ground are asking would (British Prime Minister) John Major deal with another IRA cessation the way he dealt with the last one and that's the key to the future," he said.
Adams' autobiography had a 20,000 print run for its launch in Germany and the publisher reported brisk sales.
The Sinn Fein leader said of the book, which ends with the 1981 hunger strikes by IRA prisoners: "I was a little bit self-conscious about dealing with contemporary events.
"One, they are fairly sensitive and two, I didn't want to be exploiting or even saying something that would make the current situation more fraught."
